conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’ll be giving you a quick, well-known questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in to see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, and it helps us make sure you’re getting any support you might need.  

Everything we talk about stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety, and even then we’d work together on next steps. We’ll keep this relaxed and conversational—no right or wrong answers, just honesty. When you’re ready, we can start with the first gentle question.  

<med>EPDS Q1</med>  
Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things or look forward to outings the way you normally would, or has that felt harder lately?

Honestly? It feels a lot harder. I used to get excited just about grabbing coffee with a friend or even going to Target alone, but lately it’s like… meh. I still go if someone plans something, but I’m not really looking forward to it, and when I’m there I keep thinking I should be home with the baby or worrying he’ll need me. Nothing feels as fun as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels kind of forced or fades fast. My husband will make a joke and I’ll smile, but it’s like the joy just doesn’t stick. I mostly feel too tired or pre-occupied to find things genuinely funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much, I guess. I’ll tell myself, “It’ll be nice to get out for that walk,” or, “Maybe I’ll feel better if I bake something,” but when the moment comes it just feels flat—like I’m going through the motions. Even little things I used to enjoy feel more like chores now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right or I missed some cue. Last night he wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept replaying everything—maybe I ate something that bothered him, maybe I put him down too soon. I know rationally it’s not all on me, but I still feel like I’m failing at the one job I’m supposed to be good at.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right—even though he’s perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie down and my brain starts spinning about SIDS, choking, the temperature in the room… I know most of it’s unlikely, but I can’t shut the thoughts off. Some mornings I’m already on edge before I even open my eyes.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I think something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes if I pace or do the breathing the nurse showed me, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes... most days, really. There’s always laundry, bottles to wash, the baby needing something, and I keep thinking, "I should be able to handle this." But it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Some afternoons I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, too overwhelmed to move, telling myself I’ll catch up after the next nap—and then I never do.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, it’s been rough. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed exhausted, but then my brain won’t shut off—replaying every little thing I think I did wrong or imagining worst-case scenarios. Some nights I just lie there staring at the ceiling until I hear him stir again. Even when I do fall asleep, I jerk awake for no reason, heart pounding, and then it starts all over.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, honestly. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Little tasks feel huge, and I catch myself tearing up for no real reason—like when I’m folding his onesies or warming a bottle. I keep waiting for a “good” day, but it hasn’t come.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been happening a few times a week. Sometimes it’s triggered—like when I can’t get him to stop crying or when I drop something silly—but other times it just bubbles up out of nowhere. I’ll be rocking him and tears start rolling down my face. I try to hide it so my older kid or my husband won’t see, but it’s getting harder to hold it in.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t felt that way. I get overwhelmed and I cry, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just keep wishing I could feel like “me” again, for everything to feel lighter.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening note – Postpartum depression/anxiety screen

Presenting symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, feeling “heavy” most days  
- Marked anhedonia: humor feels forced, previously pleasant activities “flat”  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive, distressing worries about infant safety; multiple daily panic-style episodes (chest tightness, shakiness)  
- Overwhelmed by routine tasks; describes “drowning” in small responsibilities  
- Initial and middle insomnia driven by rumination and “worst-case” thinking  

Pattern  
Symptoms present “most of the time,” escalating over past weeks; functional impairment notable in home management and emotional availability.

Risk factors identified  
- Postpartum period (infant <12 mo)  
- Daily sadness, crying, anhedonia, guilt, fatigue, concentration difficulty  
- Sleep disruption exceeding infant-related awakenings  
- Recurrent panic symptoms  
- No self-harm ideation reported (specifically denied)

Screening significance  
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold; meet provisional criteria for moderate–severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment, psychoeducation, support mobilization, and safety plan. No emergent self-harm concern at present.
